readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This final module tours specialized AWS services in four areas: development, business apps, end-user computing and IoT. It then introduces the AWS Well-Architected Framework and its six pillars, applies the framework to an online florist, and presents the AWS Well-Architected Tool for reviewing your own workloads. A closing real-life lesson shows how a few of these services combine into a serverless backend, a serverless contact form and a support line with callbacks.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 13 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Well-Architected Solutions: why flexible building blocks call for a way to judge design quality.

AWS Specialized Services and Solutions

  1. AWS Specialized Services: CodeBuild, CodePipeline, X-Ray, AppSync, Amplify, Amazon Connect, SES, AppStream 2.0, WorkSpaces, WorkSpaces Secure Browser and IoT Core.
  2. AWS Well-Architected Framework: the six pillars, the AWS WA Tool and a florist architecture improved pillar by pillar.

Cloud in Real Life

  1. Specialized Use Cases: a serverless backend traced by X-Ray, an S3 site whose form emails through SES, and Amazon Connect callbacks.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Every AWS service is purpose-built for particular use cases.
  • CodeBuild runs continuous integration builds, CodePipeline automates the whole CI/CD release, X-Ray lets developers visualize and debug app behavior, AppSync offers managed GraphQL APIs and Amplify speeds up full-stack web and mobile apps.
  • Amazon Connect runs AI-powered contact centers, and Amazon SES automates high-volume transactional and marketing email.
  • WorkSpaces gives a complete, persistent desktop, AppStream 2.0 streams applications rather than a whole desktop, and WorkSpaces Secure Browser covers browser-only access.
  • AWS IoT Core securely links sensor-equipped physical devices to cloud applications.
  • The Well-Architected Framework's six pillars run from Operational Excellence through Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency and Cost Optimization to Sustainability.
  • Typical pillar moves include CI/CD automation, least privilege and encryption, multiple Availability Zones, rightsizing, Spot Instances and Savings Plans, and Lambda in place of always-on servers.
  • The AWS WA Tool is free, reviews a workload against the pillars and suggests best-practice remediations you can override, but it does not migrate workloads, forecast costs or manage permissions.
  • A few managed services such as API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, SES and Amazon Connect can be recombined to solve very different problems.

readme.title: What the assessment focuses on
readme.html:
What the assessment focuses on

The module assessment has 6 questions.

  • Choosing AWS Amplify to add ready-made features to a full-stack app: 1 question.
  • Choosing Amazon SES for automated marketing email: 1 question.
  • Telling Amazon WorkSpaces (full desktop) apart from Amazon AppStream 2.0 (app streaming) for remote staff: 1 question.
  • Using AWS IoT Core to monitor physical equipment: 1 question.
  • Applying the Reliability pillar through multiple Availability Zones, with the other pillars as labelled distractors: 1 question.
  • Rightsizing an oversized EC2 instance as Performance Efficiency, which means telling it apart from pure cost cutting and from automatic scaling with demand: 1 question.
  • Look-alike services recur as distractors, so know where Amazon Connect (3 questions), Amazon AppStream 2.0 (3), AWS AppSync (2) and the AWS Well-Architected Tool (2) fit.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The recap lists the purpose-built services under development, business and customer support, although the lessons also covered end-user computing and IoT. It returns to the six Well-Architected pillars and to the AWS Well-Architected Tool as the way to assess workloads, improve them and bring them in line with best practices. It ends on serverless designs, where API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB scale and run efficiently while keeping infrastructure to a minimum. In the farewell video the hosts look back on a course that ran from Regions and Availability Zones through EC2 to database migration. Their advice: do not be daunted by how big AWS is, start from the basics and keep building, even five minutes a day.

aws-specialized-services.html:
AWS Specialized Services

Objectives

  • Match developer needs to AWS services.
  • Pick services for contact centers and bulk email.
  • Choose among remote desktop and app options.
  • Name the device service.

Notes

Purpose-built services

  • AWS shapes each service around particular jobs, often at customers' request.

Development services

  • (continuous integration and continuous delivery) builds, tests and ships each committed change automatically for fast, dependable releases.
  • : managed CI that compiles, tests and packages code, scales itself and bills only for build time.
  • : managed CI/CD that spots repository changes and runs build, test and deploy stages, shipping fixes reliably with no servers to provision.
  • : monitors and traces requests so developers can visualize app behavior, find bottlenecks, debug faster and tune efficiency and reliability.
  • : managed , one secure merging many backend data sources for frontends.
  • : speeds up building, deploying and running secure, scalable full-stack (frontend plus backend) web and mobile apps, adding sign-in, APIs, storage and hosting with little infrastructure work.

Business application services

  • : AI-powered cloud contact center for calls and chats, with call routing, recording, analytics and AWS integrations.
  • : affordable, scalable email any app can use to automate reliable bulk sends (newsletters, promotions, transactional mail) and improve delivery.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Amazon SES Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) sends transactional, marketing and bulk email straight from your applications, with .

End-user computing services

  • : streams desktop and apps (even desktop apps made SaaS with no code changes) to a browser on any device, so nothing is installed and modest hardware suffices.
  • : fully managed virtual desktop infrastructure, a complete persistent desktop staff reach securely from anywhere and use like an office PC, cost-efficient and easy to run.
  • (formerly WorkSpaces Web): a lightweight managed enterprise browser for web-only users, safely reaching private sites, SaaS apps and the open internet with no client software, infrastructure or VPNs.

IoT services

  • IoT (Internet of Things): physical devices fitted with sensors and software that gather and swap data online and can be watched and controlled remotely, for efficiency, new services and a better quality of life.
  • : that securely links devices to cloud apps and simplifies ingesting, processing and acting on their data, using mutual authentication, end-to-end encryption and a choice of protocols.

Key takeaways

  • CodeBuild does CI builds and CodePipeline the whole release, but only X-Ray visualizes and debugs app behavior.
  • AppSync just builds GraphQL data APIs, whereas Amplify is the broad full-stack web and mobile toolkit.
  • Calls, routing and analytics mean Amazon Connect; SES is email only and WorkSpaces is a desktop.
  • WorkSpaces gives a full desktop, AppStream 2.0 streams apps (the course's pick for staff SaaS access) and Secure Browser suits web-only work.
  • IoT needs a sensing physical device, managed with AWS IoT Core; a plain app or software feature does not count.

Scenarios

  • A camera that alerts your phone, a remote pet feeder or irrigation tuned to weather and soil: IoT solutions on AWS IoT Core.

Terms

  • CI/CD: Automated build, test and deploy of every code change.
  • AWS CodeBuild: Managed CI build service.
  • AWS CodePipeline: Managed CI/CD release automation.
  • AWS X-Ray: App tracing, debugging and visualization.
  • AWS AppSync: Managed GraphQL APIs.
  • GraphQL: API query language, popular in web and mobile, where clients fetch exactly the data they want.
  • AWS Amplify: Full-stack web and mobile app toolkit.
  • Full-stack application: App with a frontend and a backend.
  • Amazon Connect: AI-powered cloud contact center.
  • Amazon SES: Scalable bulk email service.
  • End-user computing: Remote staff access to desktops and apps.
  • Amazon AppStream 2.0: App streaming to any device.
  • SaaS (software as a service): Cloud-hosted apps used online with nothing to install or maintain.
  • Amazon WorkSpaces: Managed persistent cloud desktops.
  • Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser: Managed secure remote browser.
  • IoT: Internet-connected sensor devices.
  • AWS IoT Core: Secure device-to-cloud service.

aws-well-architected-framework.html:
AWS Well-Architected Framework

Objectives

  • Explain why a working design still needs tuning.
  • Describe the six pillars.
  • Say what the does and does not do.

Notes

Why keep improving

  • The framework aims past merely working, at secure, high-performing, resilient and efficient designs, with one consistent method for any workload.
  • Needs change, so the pillars keep asking you to refine processes, resize as the workload becomes clearer and trim waste.

The six pillars

  • Operational Excellence: running and monitoring systems for business value, improving processes, pipeline-automated releases and good event response.
  • Security: protection built in, with least-privilege access, intact data and guarded systems.
  • Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.
  • Performance Efficiency: sizing resources, such as an , to workload and memory needs, and revisiting that as needs move.
  • : lower spend through smarter allocation, such as cheaper specs for an underused instance and unneeded services.
  • Sustainability: energy-efficient, lower-impact designs that avoid always-on resources, like Lambda over a nonstop EC2 instance or a smaller RDS instance, cutting cost, energy and carbon.

Rightsizing: which pillar?

  • The course cites downsizing an underused instance under both Performance Efficiency and Cost Optimization.
  • Fitting capacity to the real workload is Performance Efficiency in the assessment; cutting spend via purchase options, budgets or deprovisioning is Cost Optimization.

AWS Well-Architected Tool

  • A free, self-service AWS service for reviewing and improving workloads against the six pillars.
  • You define a workload, run the review on your account and get a report of issues, each with a best-practice fix.
  • Questions can be marked not applicable and advice overridden.
  • Features: workload reviews at its core, milestone tracking and custom lenses that adapt evaluations and improvement plans.
  • and integration support teamwork and progress tracking for architects, engineers and compliance teams.
  • Result: consistent, actionable, well-documented reviews.
  • It does not migrate workloads across Regions, forecast costs ( and do) or manage permissions (IAM does, though the tool may use it for access control).

Worked example: an online florist

  • Holiday peaks (Valentine's Day, Mother's Day) test a working design of EC2 for the site, RDS for orders and customers and S3 for photos: how well does it scale?
Pillar Finding Enhancement
Operational Excellence Survive instance failures mid-rush; add and auto-rollback self-healing EC2 Auto Scaling
Security Beyond the VPC: patching, least-privilege IAM, and in transit, fine-grained access Stronger encryption and IAM policies
Reliability Already in multiple AZs; add health monitoring and automated recovery
Performance Efficiency Rightsize EC2, RDS and Lambda against waste and underprovisioning; Lambda already scales event-driven image jobs, CloudFront already speeds images worldwide
Cost Optimization Replace On-Demand with Spot for spiky traffic and for steady load; track spend live Savings Plans, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost Explorer
Sustainability Serverless and elastic resources already help; less waste helps planet and profit

Visuals

  • Pillar flashcards (two decks of three): name on the front, focus on the back.
  • Florist walkthrough (arrow-driven process): finished design first, then the starting setup and one screen per pillar with its enhancement.
  • WA Tool review screen (video): workload name, pillars, question drop-downs, an applicability toggle and per-question help.

Key takeaways

  • Pillar cues: automated releases point to Operational Excellence, least privilege and encryption to Security, multiple AZs and recovery to Reliability.
  • Fitting size to workload points to Performance Efficiency, purchase options and deprovisioning to Cost Optimization, serverless over always-on to Sustainability.
  • The free AWS WA Tool reviews workloads and suggests overridable fixes; it does not migrate, forecast costs or manage permissions.

Scenarios

  • Hand-run releases causing outages and drifting environments: a pipeline such as (Operational Excellence).

Terms

  • AWS Well-Architected Framework: AWS's six-pillar method for designing and judging architectures.
  • Well-Architected pillars: The six review areas, from Operational Excellence to Sustainability.
  • Rightsizing: Matching a resource's size to its real workload.
  • Deprovisioning: Removing an unneeded resource to end its cost.
  • AWS Well-Architected Tool (AWS WA Tool): Free self-service workload review against the pillars.
  • Custom lens: WA Tool option that tailors a review and its improvement plan.
  • AWS Compute Optimizer: Helps keep resources neither wasted nor underprovisioned.
  • AWS Cost & Usage Report: The florist's Sustainability enhancement, tied to cutting waste.

specialized-use-cases.html:
Specialized Use Cases

Objectives

  • See how mixing a few specialized AWS services solves concrete business problems.

Notes

Serverless web backend with X-Ray

  • Building blocks: Gateway in front, Lambda for logic, DynamoDB for data and X-Ray for tracing, a developer favorite.
  • A client makes an HTTP call, API Gateway checks it and starts Lambda, Lambda talks to DynamoDB and the reply heads back.
  • Work is split across services instead of one web server, so X-Ray follows each request through every hop to show which one failed.

Static S3 website with a contact form

  • The site sits in an : upload the files, switch on website hosting and it is live.
  • A submitted Contact Us form calls API Gateway, which runs Lambda to email the owner through , so no server is needed.
  • Same services as the backend, new purpose, since Lambda runs whatever code you give it.

Contact center with callbacks

  • Phone calls land in 's system, and text messages come in through CloudFront.
  • Connect first tries to put the customer through to a live agent.
  • If the queue is long, the caller can pick a callback and hang up, or continue by text with a handling the switch.
  • Chat or email can also serve as the alternate channel.
  • Connect, Lambda and CloudFront together make a smarter support desk.

Common thread

  • Recombining a handful of managed services covers very different, complex problems.

Visuals

  • Serverless backend diagram (markers: receive traffic, trigger Lambda, monitor traffic): X-Ray watching the whole request path.
  • Static website diagram (markers: customer input, request intake, email): a form-to-email flow with no web server.
  • Amazon Connect diagram (markers: first contact, agent connection, long-wait options): a callback or text sparing customers a long hold.

Key takeaways

  • API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB form a fully serverless web backend.
  • X-Ray locates failures in distributed designs by tracing requests end to end.
  • Changing only the Lambda code turns the same pattern from storing data into sending SES email.
  • Amazon Connect lets callers skip a long wait through a callback or a switch to text.

Scenarios

  • Contact form on a static site with no server: S3, API Gateway, Lambda and SES.
  • Long support hold times: Amazon Connect callbacks.

Terms

  • Serverless architecture: A design of managed services that needs no server of your own and minimal infrastructure.
  • Distributed environment: An app spread over several services rather than one web server.
  • Interactive voice response (IVR): Amazon Connect's voice front end, the first stop for calls before a live agent is tried.
  • Agent callback: Hanging up and letting an agent call back instead of waiting on hold.

Elastic Beanstalk runs a web app on managed capacity, but it does not watch the repository and chain release stages.
CodePipeline notices each repository change and carries it through the build, test and deploy stages without servers.
X-Ray traces requests in a running app, so it helps debugging rather than shipping each commit.

questions.takeaway: A developer who needs both frontend and backend for a web app, with little infrastructure work, can use AWS Amplify.

read.text: AWS Amplify: speeds up building, deploying and running secure, scalable full-stack (frontend plus backend) web and mobile apps, adding sign-in, APIs, storage and hosting with little infrastructure work.

questions.stem: The cafe's web developer can build the frontend of a new ordering site but has never set up a backend. She wants one toolkit that also gives the site its backend pieces, so she can build, deploy and run the whole app herself. Which service fits?

options.why: Lightsail offers simple, predictably priced hosting, but it does not add backend pieces such as sign-in to the app.
Amplify speeds up building, deploying and running full-stack web apps, adding the backend with little infrastructure work.
Elastic Beanstalk turns finished code into a running web environment, but it does not supply the backend features for her.
AppSync builds one GraphQL data API, which is only a single backend piece rather than a full-stack toolkit.

questions.takeaway: Customer calls and chats that need routing, recording and analytics point to Amazon Connect.

read.text: Amazon Connect: AI-powered cloud contact center for calls and chats, with call routing, recording, analytics and AWS integrations.

questions.stem: The cafe chain wants customers to phone or chat about catering orders, with each call routed to the right staff member, recorded and analyzed. Which service fits?

options.why: Lex builds conversational chatbots, but it is not a full contact center that routes and records calls to staff.
SES sends email from applications, so it cannot take phone calls or route them to staff.
SNS pushes notifications to subscribers, which does not handle live calls and chats with routing.
Connect is a cloud contact center for calls and chats, with routing, recording and analytics built in.

questions.takeaway: To see how requests move through an app and debug errors faster, developers trace them with AWS X-Ray.

read.text: AWS X-Ray: monitors and traces requests so developers can visualize app behavior, find bottlenecks, debug faster and tune efficiency and reliability.

questions.stem: Now and then, customers see an error when they redeem loyalty points, and the developers cannot reproduce it. They want to visualize how each request moves through the app so they can debug it faster. Which service fits?

options.why: AppSync gives frontends one GraphQL API over many data sources, but it does not show how requests behave while the app runs.
CloudTrail logs who made which AWS API calls, which audits the account but does not trace requests inside the app.
Amplify helps build and host full-stack apps, but it does not trace live requests to debug an error.
X-Ray monitors and traces requests so developers can visualize app behavior and debug faster.

questions.takeaway: AWS Amplify is the broad full-stack web and mobile toolkit, while AppSync only builds GraphQL data APIs.

read.text: AppSync just builds GraphQL data APIs, whereas Amplify is the broad full-stack web and mobile toolkit.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the scope of AWS Amplify?

options.text: It merges many backend data sources into one GraphQL API
options.why: A single GraphQL API over many data sources is AppSync, which is narrower than Amplify's whole-app toolkit.

options.text: It speeds up building whole web and mobile apps end to end
options.why: Amplify is the broad full-stack web and mobile toolkit, covering frontend and backend rather than one API.

options.text: It compiles, tests and packages code each time a build runs
options.why: Compiling, testing and packaging code is CodeBuild's managed CI, not Amplify's app toolkit.

options.text: It traces requests so developers can find slow backend calls
options.why: Tracing requests to find bottlenecks is X-Ray, which watches a running app rather than building one.

questions.takeaway: Amazon WorkSpaces is fully managed virtual desktop infrastructure that gives each user a persistent cloud desktop.

read.text: Amazon WorkSpaces: Managed persistent cloud desktops.

questions.stem: Which description matches Amazon WorkSpaces?

options.text: A single app streamed to any browser
options.why: Streaming single apps to a browser is AppStream 2.0, not the full desktop that WorkSpaces gives.

options.text: A persistent desktop in the cloud
options.why: WorkSpaces is fully managed virtual desktop infrastructure that gives staff a persistent cloud desktop.

options.text: A managed browser for web-only users
options.why: A lightweight managed browser for web-only users is WorkSpaces Secure Browser, a separate service.

options.text: A simple virtual server at a set price
options.why: A simple server at a set monthly price describes Lightsail, which is not a desktop service.

questions.takeaway: When developers must see where requests slow down inside an app, AWS X-Ray traces them to the bottleneck.

read.text: AWS X-Ray: monitors and traces requests so developers can visualize app behavior, find bottlenecks, debug faster and tune efficiency and reliability.

questions.stem: Checkout in the cafe's online ordering app has become slow, and the developers cannot tell which backend call causes the delay. Which service helps them trace requests and find the bottleneck?

options.why: CloudTrail records who made which API calls in the account, which audits activity but does not trace slow app requests.
X-Ray traces each request through the app, so the developers can see which call is the bottleneck.
CodePipeline ships code changes through release stages, so it cannot show where a running request slows down.
CodeBuild compiles and tests code before release, not requests while the app is serving customers.

questions.takeaway: AWS IoT Core securely links sensor devices to cloud apps and handles ingesting, processing and acting on their data.

read.text: AWS IoT Core: managed service that securely links devices to cloud apps and simplifies ingesting, processing and acting on their data, using mutual authentication, end-to-end encryption and a choice of protocols.

questions.stem: The cafe fits its coffee machines with sensors that report bean levels online, so staff can watch and adjust them from anywhere. Which jobs would AWS IoT Core take on for this project? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Connect the machines securely to the cafe's cloud apps
options.why: IoT Core is the managed service that links devices such as these machines to cloud apps, with mutual authentication and encryption.

options.text: Record supplier calls about the machines' bean orders
options.why: Recording calls is a contact center feature of Amazon Connect, not a job IoT Core does for the sensor-fitted machines.

options.text: Ingest the machines' bean readings and act on them
options.why: IoT Core simplifies ingesting, processing and acting on device data, such as the bean levels the machines report.

options.text: Trace slow requests in the app showing the machines' readings
options.why: Tracing requests to find slow spots in an app is AWS X-Ray, which does not link the machines or take in their data.

options.text: Stream the machines' stock program to managers' browsers
options.why: Streaming a program to a browser on any device is Amazon AppStream 2.0, which does not connect sensor devices to the cloud.

questions.takeaway: Among developer services, only AWS X-Ray visualizes and debugs app behavior; the Code services build and release code.

read.text: CodeBuild does CI builds and CodePipeline the whole release, but only X-Ray visualizes and debugs app behavior.

questions.stem: Among the AWS developer services, which one lets developers visualize and debug how their application behaves?

options.why: AppSync provides managed GraphQL APIs for frontends, not a view into how the app behaves at run time.
CodeBuild handles CI builds that compile and package code, not visualizing app behavior.
X-Ray is the developer service that visualizes app behavior so teams can debug and tune it.
CodePipeline automates the release of code changes, so it does not show how the app behaves.

questions.takeaway: Streaming a single desktop app to a browser with nothing installed points to AppStream 2.0, not a full WorkSpaces desktop.

read.text: Amazon AppStream 2.0: streams desktop and SaaS apps (even desktop apps made SaaS with no code changes) to a browser on any device, so nothing is installed and modest hardware suffices.

questions.stem: Office staff at the cafe need one desktop accounting app on their modest laptops. They want to open just that app in a browser with nothing installed, rather than a full desktop. Which service fits?

options.why: WorkSpaces gives each person a complete persistent desktop, which is more than one streamed app.
Secure Browser suits web-only work, but the staff need a desktop app rather than websites.
AppStream 2.0 streams a desktop app to a browser on any device, so nothing is installed and modest hardware is enough.
EC2 gives raw virtual servers the cafe would have to set up and manage, not one app streamed to staff browsers.

questions.takeaway: Sensor devices that report data and take commands remotely connect to the cloud securely through AWS IoT Core.

read.text: AWS IoT Core: managed service that securely links devices to cloud apps and simplifies ingesting, processing and acting on their data, using mutual authentication, end-to-end encryption and a choice of protocols.

questions.stem: The cafe fits its refrigerators with temperature sensors that send readings online so staff can watch them and change settings remotely. Which service securely links these devices to the cafe's cloud apps?

options.why: Kinesis Data Streams carries streaming data, but it does not authenticate devices or manage them remotely.
SNS pushes notifications to subscribers, not a secure link for sensor devices to report and take commands.
IoT Core securely connects devices to cloud apps, with mutual authentication and encryption, and acts on their data.
Lambda runs code in response to events, but it is not the service that connects and secures the sensors.

questions.takeaway: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center with call routing, recording and analytics built in for calls and chats.

read.text: Amazon Connect: AI-powered cloud contact center for calls and chats, with call routing, recording, analytics and AWS integrations.

questions.stem: The cafe is moving its customer help line onto Amazon Connect. Which features does Connect provide for that help line? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Giving each agent a persistent virtual desktop
options.why: A persistent virtual desktop for each agent is what Amazon WorkSpaces provides, not a contact center feature of Connect.

options.text: Routing each contact to the right staff member
options.why: Connect has call routing built in, so each call or chat on the help line reaches the right person.

options.text: Tracing slow requests in the cafe's web app
options.why: Tracing requests to find slow spots in an app is the job of AWS X-Ray, not a feature of the Connect contact center.

options.text: Recording each conversation for later review
options.why: Connect records calls, so the cafe can review help line conversations and feed them into analytics.

options.text: Streaming an order program to staff browsers
options.why: Streaming a program to a browser on any device is Amazon AppStream 2.0, not a contact center feature of Connect.

questions.takeaway: Operational Excellence covers running, monitoring and improving systems, including automated releases and event response.

read.text: Operational Excellence: running and monitoring systems for business value, improving processes, pipeline-automated releases and good event response.

questions.stem: Which practice belongs to the Operational Excellence pillar?

options.text: Granting each user only the access the job needs
options.why: Least-privilege access is a Security pillar practice.

options.text: Spreading the database across several Availability Zones
options.why: Running in multiple Availability Zones to recover from failure is a Reliability practice.

options.text: Monitoring systems and improving how they are run
options.why: Operational Excellence is about running and monitoring systems for business value and refining those processes.

options.text: Moving a steady workload onto a cheaper purchase option
options.why: Choosing purchase options to lower spend is a Cost Optimization practice.

questions.takeaway: The WA Tool adds custom lenses, milestones, not-applicable marking and IAM and API teamwork to its core reviews.

read.text: Features: workload reviews at its core, milestone tracking and custom lenses that adapt evaluations and improvement plans.

questions.stem: Match each AWS Well-Architected Tool feature to what it does.

pairs.right: Tailors the review and its improvement plan
pairs.why: A custom lens adapts what the review checks and the improvement plan it produces.

pairs.right: Records a workload's progress over time
pairs.why: Milestones capture the state of a workload so later reviews can show what improved.

pairs.right: Skips a question that does not fit the workload
pairs.why: A question can be marked not applicable when it has no bearing on the workload.

pairs.right: Lets several teams work and track progress together
pairs.why: IAM and API support let architects, engineers and compliance teams share the review work.

questions.takeaway: Choosing a purchase option that fits a steady load, in place of On-Demand, is a Cost Optimization lever.

read.text: Fitting capacity to the real workload is Performance Efficiency in the assessment; cutting spend via purchase options, budgets or deprovisioning is Cost Optimization.

questions.stem: The cafe's servers run On-Demand around the clock, and their load stays steady all week, month after month. Under the Cost Optimization pillar, which change fits?

options.text: Spread the servers across several Availability Zones
options.why: Multiple Availability Zones are a sound Reliability step, but they do not lower what the servers cost.

options.text: Move each server to a larger instance type
options.why: A larger instance type changes performance, not the purchase option, and it raises rather than lowers the bill.

options.text: Change the purchase option for the servers
options.why: Cutting spend by moving the steady servers off On-Demand to a better-fitting purchase option is a Cost Optimization move.

options.text: Encrypt the order data at rest and in transit
options.why: Encryption is a sound Security step, but it leaves the On-Demand spend unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Deprovisioning unneeded resources and cheaper specs for underused ones point to Cost Optimization.

read.text: Cost Optimization: lower spend through smarter allocation, such as cheaper specs for an underused instance and deprovisioning unneeded services.

questions.stem: The cafe keeps paying for a test service nobody uses anymore and for an instance that sits mostly idle. The owner deprovisions the test service and moves the instance to smaller specs, with spend as the only goal. Which pillar is the owner applying?

options.why: Deprovisioning unneeded services and smaller specs for an underused instance, done to cut spend, is Cost Optimization.
Sustainability also favors removing idle resources, but its aim is energy and carbon, and here the stated goal is spend alone.
Reliability plans recovery from failures and is not about cutting the monthly bill.
Security protects access and data, and removing an unused service here is about spend.

questions.takeaway: The Well-Architected Framework is a six-pillar method for designing and judging architectures, not a service.

read.text: AWS Well-Architected Framework: AWS's six-pillar method for designing and judging architectures.

questions.stem: What does the AWS Well-Architected Framework give a team that builds on AWS?

options.text: A free service that reviews a workload and suggests fixes
options.why: That describes the AWS Well-Architected Tool, whose question-based review applies the framework rather than being it.

options.text: A six-pillar method for designing and judging designs
options.why: The framework is a consistent, six-pillar way to design an architecture and assess how well it holds up.

options.text: A phased plan for moving a business into the cloud
options.why: A migration plan is a different kind of guidance and does not score a design against pillars.

options.text: A pricing model that rewards a steady usage commitment
options.why: A pricing model lowers a bill, while the framework is a method for judging the architecture itself.

questions.takeaway: The free AWS Well-Architected Tool reviews a workload against the six pillars and suggests a fix for each issue.

read.text: A free, self-service AWS service for reviewing and improving workloads against the six pillars.

questions.stem: The cafe's architect wants a free AWS service that reviews the ordering workload against the six pillars and reports each issue with a best-practice fix. Which service fits?

options.why: Config tracks resource settings against rules, not a pillar-by-pillar review of the workload.
This service gathers data about on-premises servers for a migration, not a pillar review.
The WA Tool is the free self-service review of a defined workload against the six pillars, with a fix for each issue.
Cost Explorer views and forecasts spend and does not review the design against the pillars.

questions.takeaway: Fitting a resource's size to the workload's real needs, and revisiting it, is Performance Efficiency.

read.text: Performance Efficiency: sizing resources, such as an EC2 instance, to workload and memory needs, and revisiting that as needs move.

questions.stem: After a month of running the cafe's inventory app on an EC2 instance, the team sees that memory is the bottleneck. They pick an instance size that fits the app's memory needs and plan to check again as usage changes. Which pillar does this follow?

options.why: Reliability plans recovery from failures, while this change fits the instance to the workload.
Operational Excellence improves how systems are run and released, not how an instance is sized.
Security protects access and data, and choosing an instance size for memory is not a protection measure.
Sizing the instance to the app's memory needs and revisiting it as needs move is Performance Efficiency.

questions.takeaway: Automating releases to stop hand-run outages and drift is an Operational Excellence improvement.

read.text: Hand-run releases causing outages and drifting environments: a CI/CD pipeline such as AWS CodePipeline (Operational Excellence).

questions.stem: Staff push menu updates to the cafe's site by hand, so each release follows different steps and the test and live setups drift apart. The owner adds an automated release pipeline so every release runs the same way. Which pillar does this change serve?

options.why: Performance Efficiency sizes resources to the workload, not how releases are run.
Automating releases through a pipeline improves how the cafe runs and changes its systems, which is Operational Excellence.
Security covers access and data protection, and a release pipeline is not mainly a protection measure.
Cost Optimization lowers spend, while the pipeline's aim here is safer, repeatable releases.

questions.takeaway: Sizing a resource up to fit its real workload, even at higher cost, is a Performance Efficiency choice.

read.text: Performance Efficiency: sizing resources, such as an EC2 instance, to workload and memory needs, and revisiting that as needs move.

questions.stem: The cafe's order database is underprovisioned and slows down during the lunch rush, though it never fails. The team moves it to a larger size that fits the real workload, accepting a higher bill. Which pillar does this change follow?

options.why: The change raises spend rather than lowering it, so it is not a Cost Optimization move.
Sizing the database to fit its real workload, here a lunch-rush load it could not keep up with, is Performance Efficiency.
The database never fails, so there is no recovery from failure to plan; the issue is a size that does not fit the load.
A larger always-on database uses more energy, so energy and carbon are not what this change targets.

questions.takeaway: Budgets, spending alerts and live cost tracking are Cost Optimization practices.

read.text: Fitting capacity to the real workload is Performance Efficiency in the assessment; cutting spend via purchase options, budgets or deprovisioning is Cost Optimization.

questions.stem: The cafe owner sets a monthly budget with alerts and checks the AWS bill each week, so she can act before it passes the limit. Which pillar does this practice support?

options.why: Performance Efficiency fits capacity to the workload, while this practice only watches and limits spend.
Operational Excellence covers running systems and automated releases, not tracking the bill against a limit.
Setting budgets and tracking spend as it happens are ways to lower and control cost under this pillar.
Sustainability aims to cut energy use and carbon, while a spending alert targets the bill alone.

questions.takeaway: The Sustainability pillar is about energy-efficient designs with a smaller environmental footprint.

read.text: Sustainability: energy-efficient, lower-impact designs that avoid always-on resources, like Lambda over a nonstop EC2 instance or a smaller RDS instance, cutting cost, energy and carbon.

questions.stem: Which pillar focuses on energy-efficient designs that lower a workload's environmental impact?

options.why: Performance Efficiency fits resources to the workload's needs rather than targeting environmental impact.
Reliability plans recovery from failures and is not aimed at energy use.
Cost Optimization targets spend, even though lower waste can also save energy.
Sustainability is the pillar for energy-efficient, lower-impact designs.

questions.takeaway: The Security pillar builds in protection through least-privilege access and encryption at rest and in transit.

read.text: Security: protection built in, with least-privilege access, intact data and guarded systems.

questions.stem: Which practices belong to the Security pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploying the workload across several Availability Zones
options.why: Multiple Availability Zones help a workload survive a failure, which is a Reliability practice.

options.text: Giving every identity only the permissions it needs
options.why: Least-privilege access limits what each identity can do, a core Security practice.

options.text: Releasing changes through an automated pipeline
options.why: Automated releases improve how systems are run, which is Operational Excellence.

options.text: Encrypting data at rest and while it is in transit
options.why: Encryption keeps data protected and intact, which the Security pillar asks for.

options.text: Planning automated recovery when a component fails
options.why: Planning recovery from failures is the heart of the Reliability pillar, not Security.

options.text: Updating runbooks after each software release
options.why: Keeping runbooks current as releases go out improves how systems are run, which is Operational Excellence.

questions.takeaway: Replacing always-on resources with serverless ones like Lambda is a Sustainability improvement.

read.text: Sustainability: energy-efficient, lower-impact designs that avoid always-on resources, like Lambda over a nonstop EC2 instance or a smaller RDS instance, cutting cost, energy and carbon.

questions.stem: The cafe resizes receipt images a few minutes each hour on an EC2 instance that runs nonstop. To cut energy use and carbon, which change fits the Sustainability pillar?

options.text: Move the job to AWS Lambda
options.why: Lambda runs only when the job does, avoiding an always-on instance and its energy use.

options.text: Move the job to a larger EC2 instance
options.why: A larger instance that still runs nonstop uses more energy, not less.

options.text: Move the job to Amazon Lightsail
options.why: A Lightsail server is still always on between jobs, so the idle energy use remains.

options.text: Move the job to an EC2 Reserved Instance
options.why: A Reserved Instance changes the price, but the instance still runs nonstop and uses energy while idle.

questions.takeaway: The Reliability pillar centers on planning recovery from failures and adapting as needs grow.

read.text: Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.

questions.stem: Which focus belongs to the Reliability pillar?

options.text: Matching an instance's size to its memory needs
options.why: Fitting resource size to the workload is a Performance Efficiency focus.

options.text: Planning how the system recovers from failures
options.why: Reliability is about planning recovery from failures and adapting as needs grow.

options.text: Granting each role only the access it needs
options.why: Least-privilege access is a Security focus, not recovery from failure.

options.text: Releasing changes through an automated pipeline
options.why: Automated releases improve how systems are run, which is an Operational Excellence focus.

questions.takeaway: A working design still gets revisited, because changing needs call for refining, resizing and cutting waste.

read.text: Needs change, so the pillars keep asking you to refine processes, resize as the workload becomes clearer and trim waste.

questions.stem: The cafe's online ordering site already works well, yet the owner still reviews it against the Well-Architected pillars every few months. Why does the framework encourage this?

options.text: Regions hold several AZs, so a site can run in more than one
options.why: This is true of AWS infrastructure, but it says nothing about why a working design gets reviewed again.

options.text: AWS runs the data centers, so the cafe never buys its own servers
options.why: This is true of the cloud model, but it is not the reason the framework asks for repeat reviews.

options.text: Workloads change, so sizes and processes drift from what fits
options.why: As the ordering site's workload becomes clearer and changes, the pillars push the owner to refine, resize and trim waste.

options.text: AWS secures the hardware, so the cafe guards only its own layer
options.why: This is true under the shared responsibility model, but it does not explain revisiting the design.

questions.takeaway: Least-privilege access and encryption of data point to the Security pillar.

read.text: Security: protection built in, with least-privilege access, intact data and guarded systems.

questions.stem: The cafe's loyalty database stores customer emails. The owner wants each staff role to have only the permissions it needs and the data encrypted at rest and in transit. Which pillar guides these choices?

options.why: Least-privilege permissions and encryption build protection into the design, which is the Security pillar.
Reliability plans recovery from failures and does not decide who may read the customer emails.
Operational Excellence improves how systems are run and released, not how the data is protected.
Performance Efficiency fits resource size to the workload and does not cover permissions or encryption.

questions.takeaway: Multiple Availability Zones, automated recovery and adapting to growth point to the Reliability pillar.

read.text: Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.

questions.stem: The cafe's order system must keep working if one Availability Zone fails, recover on its own, and keep up as new cafe locations open. Which pillar is the owner focusing on?

options.why: Performance Efficiency sizes resources to the workload, but planning recovery from failure belongs elsewhere.
Cost Optimization lowers spend and does not plan how the order system survives a failure.
Planning recovery from failures and adapting as the business grows is the Reliability pillar.
Sustainability reduces energy use and impact, not the order system's ability to recover.

labs.title: Specialized service per use case
labs.brief: The cafe has grown into a small chain, and its wish list now spans the app team, the support desk, the back office and the kitchen equipment. Sort each need under the purpose-built AWS service made for that job.

cards.text: Every change pushed to the ordering app's repository built, tested and deployed with no manual step
A menu-page fix that moves through build, test and deploy stages on its own once it is committed
Finding which hop of the order service slows checkout during the lunch rush
A picture of how one loyalty request travels across the app's services, to see where it broke
A new mobile preorder app with sign-in, storage and hosting, built with little infrastructure work
A full-stack catering web app, frontend and backend, built and deployed quickly by a small team
A support phone line that routes callers to the right staff member and records the calls
Callers stuck in a long queue offered a callback instead of waiting on hold
The weekly newsletter and seasonal promotions emailed to every loyalty member
A receipt email the ordering app sends automatically after each purchase
The stock-count desktop app opened in a browser on the old back-room laptops, with nothing installed
Part-time staff reaching the shift-planning app from a browser on whatever device they have
A complete, persistent office desktop the manager reaches securely from home
A full cloud desktop for each office worker, used just like the PC on their desk
Fridge temperature sensors that send readings online so staff can watch them remotely
Coffee grinders fitted with sensors that report use and can be switched from the back office

goals.label: Release and tracing needs sit under CodePipeline and X-Ray
goals.hint: Ask whether the need is shipping each committed change through its stages, or seeing how a request behaves once it runs.

goals.label: Both new-app builds sit under AWS Amplify
goals.hint: Ask whether the team is building a whole web or mobile app, frontend and backend, and wants sign-in and hosting handled for it.

goals.label: Calls sit under Amazon Connect and mailings under Amazon SES
goals.hint: Ask whether a customer is talking to the cafe live by phone or chat, or the app is simply sending email out.

goals.label: Streamed apps and full desktops sit under their own services
goals.hint: Ask whether the worker needs one app in a browser with nothing installed, or a complete desktop that keeps their files.

goals.label: Both sensor jobs sit under AWS IoT Core
goals.hint: Ask whether a physical device with sensors gathers data and sends it online to be watched or controlled.

Amazon Connect is the contact center for calls, routing and callbacks, and Amazon SES only sends email from an app.
AppStream 2.0 streams a single app to a browser, while WorkSpaces gives each worker a full persistent desktop.

SNS pushes notifications to subscribers, which does not handle live calls and chats with routing.

labs.title: Well-Architected review of the cafe
labs.brief: The cafe's systems all run, but before the holiday rush the owner had them reviewed against the AWS Well-Architected Framework, and the report lists six findings. Name the pillar each finding belongs to, then pick the fix for two of them. Each resizing finding states its aim, so judge it by what that change is meant to achieve.

spec.source: Well-Architected review, cafe systems, findings report

cells.finding: Every barista signs in to the order console with one shared admin login that can change anything
cells.concern: Anyone at the counter could edit prices or erase the order history

cells.finding: The kitchen screen server is sized far beyond the orders it handles all day
cells.concern: Capacity review: match the server's size to the orders it really handles

cells.finding: Updates to the ordering app are copied to the server by hand, and two recent hand updates broke checkout
cells.concern: Each release depends on whoever is on shift and is never done the same way twice

cells.finding: A server runs day and night to build the weekly stock report, a job of a few minutes each Sunday
cells.concern: Cut the energy and carbon of capacity that sits idle almost all week

cells.finding: The order server is one instance in one Availability Zone, with no plan to bring it back if it fails
cells.concern: If that instance or its zone fails, every order stops and nothing elsewhere can take over

cells.finding: The loyalty report server idles on large specs, and a test server nobody has used since spring still runs
cells.concern: Lower the monthly spend; speed and capacity are fine as they are

questions.prompt: Which pillar does finding F1, the shared admin login, belong to?
Which pillar does finding F2, the kitchen screen server, belong to?
Which pillar does finding F3, the hand-copied app updates, belong to?
Which pillar does finding F4, the weekly stock report server, belong to?
Which pillar does finding F5, the single order server, belong to?
Which pillar does finding F6, the idle loyalty report server and old test server, belong to?
Which change answers finding F3 on the ordering app's updates?

options.label: An automated pipeline that builds, tests and deploys each change
A larger instance for the ordering app's server
A monthly AWS WA Tool review of the ordering app
A second copy of the server in another Availability Zone

questions.prompt: Which change answers finding F4 on the weekly stock report?

options.label: Run the report as AWS Lambda code only when it is due
Move the report to a larger instance that finishes sooner
Keep the server on all week and give it more memory
Add a second always-on server in another Availability Zone

goals.label: F1 to F3 each sit under their one pillar
goals.hint: Ask what each finding is trying to achieve; for a resizing finding, read its stated aim before its subject.

goals.label: F4 to F6 each sit under their one pillar
goals.hint: Ask whether a change is made to fit the workload, to lower the bill, to cut energy, or to recover from a failure.

goals.label: The release and stock report findings get their fixes
goals.hint: Ask which change removes the cause of the finding, rather than only reviewing it or adding capacity it does not need.

lines: A design that runs is not yet well designed, so the review judges it pillar by pillar and finds work in each one.
Resizing to fit the real workload is Performance Efficiency, while the same move made to cut spend is Cost Optimization.
A fix removes the cause a finding names, such as a pipeline for hand-run releases or Lambda for a job that runs a few minutes a week.
The AWS WA Tool reports issues with best-practice fixes, but making the changes is still the cafe's job.

questions.takeaway: Fitting a resource's size to the workload's real needs, and revisiting it, is Performance Efficiency.

read.text: Performance Efficiency: sizing resources, such as an EC2 instance, to workload and memory needs, and revisiting that as needs move.

questions.stem: After a month of running the cafe's inventory app on an EC2 instance, the team sees that memory is the bottleneck. They pick an instance size that fits the app's memory needs and plan to check again as usage changes. Which pillar does this follow?

options.why: Reliability plans recovery from failures, while this change fits the instance to the workload.
Operational Excellence improves how systems are run and released, not how an instance is sized.
Security protects access and data, and choosing an instance size for memory is not a protection measure.
Sizing the instance to the app's memory needs and revisiting it as needs move is Performance Efficiency.

questions.takeaway: Deprovisioning unneeded resources and cheaper specs for underused ones point to Cost Optimization.

read.text: Cost Optimization: lower spend through smarter allocation, such as cheaper specs for an underused instance and deprovisioning unneeded services.

questions.stem: The cafe keeps paying for a test service nobody uses anymore and for an instance that sits mostly idle. The owner deprovisions the test service and moves the instance to smaller specs, with spend as the only goal. Which pillar is the owner applying?

options.why: Deprovisioning unneeded services and smaller specs for an underused instance, done to cut spend, is Cost Optimization.
Sustainability also favors removing idle resources, but its aim is energy and carbon, and here the stated goal is spend alone.
Reliability plans recovery from failures and is not about cutting the monthly bill.
Security protects access and data, and removing an unused service here is about spend.

questions.takeaway: Multiple Availability Zones, automated recovery and adapting to growth point to the Reliability pillar.

read.text: Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.

questions.stem: The cafe's order system must keep working if one Availability Zone fails, recover on its own, and keep up as new cafe locations open. Which pillar is the owner focusing on?

options.why: Performance Efficiency sizes resources to the workload, but planning recovery from failure belongs elsewhere.
Cost Optimization lowers spend and does not plan how the order system survives a failure.
Planning recovery from failures and adapting as the business grows is the Reliability pillar.
Sustainability reduces energy use and impact, not the order system's ability to recover.

incidents.title: Friday orders that failed at random
incidents.brief: On Friday evening, some orders in the cafe's loyalty app started failing at random, and a hurried fix copied to the servers by hand made things worse. The developers want to find the fault and make sure the next fix goes out safely.

steps.takeaway: To follow requests through an app and find where they stall or fail, use AWS X-Ray.

read.text: AWS X-Ray: monitors and traces requests so developers can visualize app behavior, find bottlenecks, debug faster and tune efficiency and reliability.

steps.stem: Each loyalty app order passes through several backend services before it is saved, and some orders now fail at random. The developers want to follow single requests through the app and see where they stall or break. Which service fits?

options.why: CodeBuild compiles, tests and packages code, and it does not follow live requests through the running app.
X-Ray traces each request across the app's services, so the developers can see where orders stall or fail.
AppSync builds a GraphQL API over data sources, and it gives no view of how requests behave inside the app.
CodePipeline runs the release stages for code changes, and it does not trace requests in the running app.

steps.takeaway: CodeBuild handles builds and tests, while CodePipeline automates the whole release, deploy stage included.

read.text: AWS CodePipeline: managed CI/CD that spots repository changes and runs build, test and deploy stages, shipping fixes reliably with no servers to provision.

steps.stem: The cafe's developers use AWS CodeBuild to compile and test each change to the loyalty app, but someone still copies each build to the servers by hand, and that copy step is where Friday's fix went wrong. Which service takes a change from the repository all the way to a deployed release with no manual step?

options.why: CodeBuild is what the team already has, and it covers the build and tests but not the deploy stage.
X-Ray traces requests in a running app, and it does not move code changes into production.
CodePipeline spots each repository change and runs the build, test and deploy stages, removing the hand copy.
AppSync creates a GraphQL API for frontends, and it has no part in building or deploying releases.

steps.takeaway: Learning from how a team handled an event and improving its process belongs to Operational Excellence.

read.text: Operational Excellence: running and monitoring systems for business value, improving processes, pipeline-automated releases and good event response.

steps.stem: Once the loyalty app is stable again, the team meets to go over how they spotted and handled Friday's failures, and they rewrite their response steps for the next event. Which Well-Architected pillar does this practice belong to?

options.why: Security is about least-privilege access and protected data, and these failures were not a security matter.
Performance Efficiency sizes resources to the workload, while this review changes how the team works.
This pillar covers running systems, improving processes and responding well to events, as the review does.
Sustainability aims at energy-efficient designs, and this review is about the team's event process.

incidents.title: Catering orders swamp the shop phone
incidents.brief: The cafe's new catering service is a hit. Customers ring the one shop phone all day, orders get scribbled on paper, and nobody remembers to confirm them. The owner wants the whole catering flow online before the party season.

steps.takeaway: For a whole full-stack web or mobile app built with little setup, choose Amplify, since AppSync covers only the API.

read.text: AWS Amplify: speeds up building, deploying and running secure, scalable full-stack (frontend plus backend) web and mobile apps, adding sign-in, APIs, storage and hosting with little infrastructure work.

steps.stem: A freelance developer will build the cafe's catering order site. Customers will sign in, browse platters and place orders, so the site needs a frontend, a backend API, storage and hosting, all set up with little infrastructure work. Which service fits the whole build?

options.why: AppSync builds a GraphQL API over data sources, which covers only one piece of this full-stack site.
Amplify builds, deploys and runs full-stack web apps, adding sign-in, APIs, storage and hosting with little setup.
CodeBuild compiles and tests code, and it gives the site no sign-in, storage or hosting of its own.
X-Ray traces requests in an app that already runs, and it does not help build the site in the first place.

steps.takeaway: Incoming calls that must reach a free staff member, with reports on call volume, point to Amazon Connect.

read.text: Amazon Connect: AI-powered cloud contact center for calls and chats, with call routing, recording, analytics and AWS integrations.

steps.stem: On busy days, callers to the catering line wait on hold while one person answers and the other staff never hear the phone. The owner wants the line run in the cloud, each call sent to whichever staff member is free, and reports on call volume to plan shifts. Which service fits?

options.why: SES sends email from applications, and it cannot answer phone calls or route them to free staff.
WorkSpaces gives staff a cloud desktop, and it does not take customer calls or report on them.
SNS pushes messages out to subscribers, and it does not queue incoming calls or route them to staff.
Connect is a cloud contact center that routes each call to a free agent and gives analytics on call activity.

steps.takeaway: Email that an app sends on its own, such as order confirmations, at pay-as-you-go prices points to Amazon SES.

read.text: Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) sends transactional, marketing and bulk email straight from your applications, with pay-as-you-go pricing.

steps.stem: Each catering order should make the order site send a confirmation email, plus a reminder the day before the event. Order volume swings with the seasons, and the owner wants to pay only for the mail actually sent. Which service fits?

options.why: Connect handles calls and chats in a contact center, and it is not the way an app sends its own email.
SES lets the site send transactional email itself, and its pay-as-you-go pricing follows the seasonal volume.
AppSync gives frontends a GraphQL API over data, and it does not deliver any email to customers.
WorkSpaces gives staff a cloud desktop, which would leave someone sending each email by hand.

incidents.title: Reviewing the site after the holiday rush
incidents.brief: The cafe's ordering site made it through the holiday rush, but only just. One web server crashed mid-afternoon and pages crawled at the peak. Before next year, the owner wants a structured review of the design and a clear list of what to improve.

steps.takeaway: A question-led review of one workload that returns issues with best-practice fixes is the WA Tool, not an automated checker.

read.text: You define a workload, run the review on your account and get a report of issues, each with a best-practice fix.

steps.stem: For the review, the cafe's architect wants to define the ordering site as a workload, work through design questions about it pillar by pillar, flag the ones that are irrelevant to the cafe and get back a list of issues, each paired with a suggested fix. Which AWS offering fits this review?

options.why: Trusted Advisor runs automated best-practice checks on the account, but it asks no design questions about a workload.
Compute Optimizer flags compute that is too large or too small, and it runs no question-led review of the whole design.
The WA Tool lets the architect define the site as a workload, answer and skip questions, and get issues with fixes.
The Framework is the six-pillar method itself, with no place to define the site as a workload and record answers.

steps.takeaway: Planning how a workload recovers from failures, such as automated recovery after a crash, is the Reliability pillar.

read.text: Reliability: planning recovery from failures and adapting as business and customer needs grow.

steps.stem: The review notes that when one web server crashed during the rush, the site stayed broken until a staff member noticed and restarted it by hand. The proposed fix adds health monitoring and automated recovery. Which Well-Architected pillar does this finding fall under?

options.why: Reliability plans how a workload recovers from failures, and automated recovery after a crash is exactly that.
Security covers least privilege and protecting data, and a crashed server with no attacker is not that issue.
Cost Optimization lowers spend, while this fix is about bringing the site back after a failure.
Sustainability cuts energy use and waste, and it does not plan how the site recovers from a crash.

steps.takeaway: Fitting each resource's capacity to its real workload is Performance Efficiency, while cutting spend through purchase options is Cost Optimization.

read.text: Performance Efficiency: sizing resources, such as an EC2 instance, to workload and memory needs, and revisiting that as needs move.

steps.stem: To deal with the slow pages, the review recommends checking whether each EC2 instance, the database and the Lambda functions are sized to their real workloads, then checking again as demand moves. The goal is faster pages, and the cafe keeps the same purchase options. Which pillar does this recommendation follow?

options.why: Cost Optimization cuts spend through purchase options, budgets or deprovisioning, which this fix leaves alone.
Reliability plans recovery from failures, and here nothing fails, since resources are only the wrong size.
Fitting each resource to its real workload and revisiting the fit as needs move is Performance Efficiency.
Security protects access and data, and resource sizing for speed does not touch either one.
